analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to pay cash compensation for long delays, refund cancelled flights, and end forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Senator Blumenthal with 4 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on November 17, 2021 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a set of enforceable rights for airline passengers into law. Airlines would have had to automatically refund tickets and, for long carrier-caused delays, pay up to $1,350 in cash plus meal and hotel costs; passengers bumped from oversold flights would be owed at least $1,350. It would have required fees for bags, seat selection, and changes to be proportional to the airline's actual costs, frozen seat-size reductions until minimum seat dimensions were set, banned forced arbitration and class-action waivers in ticket and frequent-flyer contracts, and given passengers and state attorneys general the right to sue airlines in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers. Passengers bumped from oversold flights would be owed a minimum of $1,350 in cash. Passengers whose arrival is delayed more than an hour by a carrier-caused problem would get an automatic ticket refund, rebooking at no cost, and for delays over four hours, $1,350 in cash plus a meal and, for overnight delays, a hotel room. All travelers would benefit from fee rules, full price disclosure including the lowest fares, guaranteed free working lavatories and potable water, refunds for damaged checked bags, and the ability to sue or join class actions instead of being forced into arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Airlines must pay involuntary bumping victims at least $1,350 in cash, and delay compensation of $1,350 plus meals and hotel costs when a carrier-caused delay exceeds four hours, with automatic refunds for any arrival delay over one hour.

Regulators must bar fees for bags, seat selection, changes, and cancellations that are unreasonable or disproportionate to the airline's actual costs, and require disclosure of the lowest available fares and all taxes and fees at the point of sale.
The FAA must prohibit any reduction in seat size, legroom, or aisle width until it sets minimum seat dimensions, and airlines must guarantee free, working lavatories and free potable water on board.

Pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in ticket, frequent-flyer, and airline credit-product contracts become unenforceable, and passengers and state attorneys general get a private right of action against unfair or deceptive practices and discrimination.

Civil penalties for passenger-protection violations are freed from the statutory cap, airlines cannot negotiate reductions with the FAA, and a study would examine paying those penalties directly to affected passengers.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines and their shareholders, through cash compensation payouts, refunds, fee restrictions, penalty exposure, and litigation risk; some of these costs would likely be passed on to ticket prices over time.

drawbacks.text: The mandates are costly to airlines, and carriers would likely pass some of that cost to consumers through higher base fares, offsetting part of the savings from the fee restrictions.

Automatically owing $1,350 for any arrival delay over four hours attributed to the carrier is more generous than comparable European rules, and the line between a 'carrier-controlled' delay and weather is disputed ground; the bill tries to police this by making it an unfair practice to blame weather for delays the carrier actually controlled, but that determination would still be contentious in practice.

Freezing seat dimensions and setting minimums by regulation could constrain the ultra-low-cost business model that keeps some base fares low, and critics argued such terms belong in market competition rather than statute.
Overriding pre-dispute arbitration and class-action waivers runs against decades of federal arbitration law, inviting legal challenges and industry litigation over every provision.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly half of Americans who fly in a given year, the direct benefits are concrete: cash when an airline strands them, refunds without having to ask, and honest all-in pricing. The costs are real but diffuse — somewhat higher fares as airlines absorb compensation mandates and lose their most profitable fee practices — and the most aggressive provisions, like the blanket $1,350 delay payment, would have faced genuine operational and legal friction. On balance the bill traded airline revenue for passenger rights, and its design questions were never tested because it never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the 117th Congress ended and it expired.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the Airline Passengers' Bill of Rights in the Senate on November 17, 2021, joined by Senators Markey, Whitehouse, Wyden, and Casey.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
That referral is the last action of any kind in the bill's history; the committee never considered it and the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill's cosponsor list shows 4 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. airlines are better off. Without the bill, they kept forced arbitration and class-action waivers in ticket contracts, kept fee and seating practices free of statutory limits, and faced no mandated cash compensation for delays and bumped passengers.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 17, 2021 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Major U.S. passenger airlines
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory cash compensation for delays, limits on ancillary fees, and bans on forced arbitration in consumer contracts through industry lobbying in the period around this bill's introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were Democrats — 4 of 48 Senate Democratic cosponsors plus the sponsor — no Republican signed on, and with no recorded vote the partisan split was never tested on the floor.

industries.note: Airlines would lose forced arbitration, uncapped penalties for passenger-protection violations, freedom to charge fees unrelated to cost, and the ability to shrink seats — with mandated cash compensation up to $1,350 for long delays and bumped passengers. Ancillary fees and the arbitration system are major revenue and cost-shielding mechanisms for the industry.

industries.industry: Online travel agencies and flight metasearch engines
industries.note: The bill would bar airlines from withholding schedule, fare, and fee data from these platforms and require airlines to let consumers complete purchases through them, strengthening their role as price-comparison channels.

The bill would invalidate pre-dispute arbitration and class-action waivers in airline reward-program and credit-product contracts, exposing card and loyalty programs to consumer class actions they are currently shielded from.
